strategy_name: Dual price+time stop discipline with horizon-matched expiry
mechanism: Time-decay-sensitive positions require a time stop set at setup equal to the forecast horizon, independent of the price stop; if either is hit the thesis is dead.
setup_summary: Every position must be entered with both a price stop and a time stop stated up front; the time stop equals the forecast horizon (e.g., 'breakout this week' — if by the end of the forecast window the move has not occurred, exit). In V8 terms: expiry_bars is a thesis-invalidation (still_valid=false at time expiry), not merely a parameter.
trigger_invalidation: Rule-level: exit on price-stop hit OR time-stop hit (whichever first). The failure mode being prevented is hope-based holding ('tomorrow, definitely tomorrow'), which lets time decay and delta-flip destroy a correct-direction position.
risk_geometry: Expiry_bars set at setup = forecast horizon; if forecast timing is hazy, extend the window deliberately at cost ('buy extra time' with a further expiration) rather than extending silently mid-trade; price stop is separate from time stop.
quote: it is important to have both price and time stop-loss levels. If either is hit, the trader should exit the trade. For example... If by the close of business Friday the move has not taken place, he should exit the trade.
chapter_anchor: Ch. 8 Trade Management, pp. 246
notes: Confirms and sharpens V8's existing expiry_bars lifecycle rule: the book makes time-stop a hard, pre-committed invalidation and explicitly couples it to the forecast horizon. Also gives the 'buy extra time' policy for uncertain timing — a risk_geometry variant, not a mid-trade decision.
book: Option Spread Strategies - Trading Up, Down, and Sideways Markets 2009

strategy_name: Lines-in-the-sand invalidation (boundary breach or velocity overrun kills thesis)
mechanism: Support/resistance boundaries anchored at setup are 'lines in the sand': if the price crosses them, or moves with greater velocity/magnitude than forecast, the forecast is falsified and action is mandatory.
setup_summary: Extends V8's still_valid dead-thesis logic: a thesis is invalidated not only by a level-crossing but also by a velocity/magnitude overrun versus the forecast at setup. Both conditions require immediate modification or exit — 'the investor cannot play mind games with this type of position and must act immediately.'
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: (a) anchor boundary penetrated, or (b) realized bar velocity/magnitude exceeds the forecast band. Consequence: exit or restructure the position without delay.
risk_geometry: Frozen anchor levels (S/R or congestion zones) recorded at setup as risk-management anchors; breach of an anchor or of a velocity bound is an automatic exit trigger; this is distinct from the price stop (which is a fixed loss limit, not a thesis boundary).
quote: If they are penetrated, or if the underlying price begins to move with a greater velocity and in greater magnitudes than the trader had forecast, it is time for him to look for the exit because his forecast is incorrect.
chapter_anchor: Ch. 7 Trade Management, p. 217
notes: Crypto 24/7 amplification: a velocity-overrun invalidation catches liquidation-accelerated moves that a fixed stop at the level alone would miss. Refines V8's existing still_valid semantics rather than proposing a new expert.
book: Option Spread Strategies - Trading Up, Down, and Sideways Markets 2009

strategy_name: Partial-profit scaling with phase-end detection
mechanism: Extract profit progressively as a winning move develops (scaling out / rolling into profits) while keeping residual exposure; exit the residual when the move shows phase-end signals (deceleration, old S/R, vol drop).
setup_summary: Rule for winning positions: scale out a portion at defined milestones as the position moves in favor (book: 'He can slowly scale out of the position as it goes in his favor. This action takes profits and limits remaining risk.'), and treat deceleration / old support-resistance / declining volatility as signals the current phase is ending — exit rather than 'stay too long at the party.'
trigger_invalidation: Trigger to reduce: profit milestone reached; phase-end signal present. Invalidation of the scaling decision: forecast continues to call for high-magnitude movement — then rolling keeps exposure ('maintaining market exposure') instead of exiting.
risk_geometry: Scale-out fraction and milestone levels defined at setup; remaining risk re-evaluated at each scale point; final exit on phase-end signal or stop, not on hope.
quote: Take Partial Profits... slowly scale out of the position as it goes in his favor. This action takes profits and limits remaining risk.
chapter_anchor: Ch. 7 Trade Management, p. 213; Ch. 8 Trade Management, pp. 244-245
notes: V8's ExposureBook allows partial exits within the one-exposure-per-direction rule; this finding adds the phase-end detection trigger (slowdown at old S/R, vol drop) for the residual exit. Options-specific 'rolling' mechanics are dropped; only the sizing/exit discipline transfers.

strategy_name: Event-risk admission gate (bounded-risk geometry for modest capital)
mechanism: Positions with open-ended adverse risk expose capital to event risk — a large market-moving event can move price so fast that no exit is possible, turning a thesis-error into a catastrophic loss.
setup_summary: RiskGate admission rule: any strategy whose loss is unbounded when a boundary is breached (ratio-spread analog) is gated by an event-risk test — if capital is modest, or overnight/weekend event risk is not tolerable, the trade must be structured with bounded (fixed-R) geometry or declined.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: candidate strategy has open-ended risk on the adverse side. Resolution: either convert to bounded-risk geometry (book: 'The spread can be capped and turned into a limited-risk butterfly') or reject admission.
risk_geometry: Max adverse loss capped at setup; no naked open-ended short exposure; event risk considered continuous (in perp crypto there are no exchange closing gaps, but funding spikes, flash crashes and liquidation cascades are the equivalent event risk on a 24/7 market).
quote: Event risk occurs when a large, market-moving event causes the underlying in which the trader has a ratio spread to gap through her short strikes, leaving no chance to exit the trade or manage risk...
chapter_anchor: Ch. 7 Trade Management, p. 212
notes: V8 already enforces bounded-risk geometry and one-exposure rules; this finding adds the explicit event-risk admission test and the continuous-risk view (crypto has no gaps but has 24/7 event risk), aligning with V8's risk-percent and heat-cap discipline.

strategy_name: Point-in-Time Release-Lag Discipline in COT Backtests
mechanism: signals are only actionable when the data existed and was released; using compilation dates instead of release dates, or applying a different lag in testing than live, invalidates backtests
setup_summary: COT files carry Tuesday compilation dates but were released later: 6-business-day lag pre-1990, 3-day nominal/10-day skip-week lag from Oct 1992, weekly Friday release of prior-Tuesday positions only since Oct 9 2000, and Options+Futures Combined-report publication parity only since Jan 18 2002. Any backtest that enters on the next weekly open after a COT signal must apply the contemporaneous release lag; results generated without it are, in the author's words, 'imaginary.'
trigger_invalidation: N/A
risk_geometry: N/A
quote: If you see system testing that took a position on the next weekly open after a COT signal was generated, you will know that the testing prior to 2002 is invalid. (Those kinds of results are not just hypothetical, they are imaginary.)
chapter_anchor: Appendix B, 'Data Periodicity and Lag'
notes: Directly mirrors V8's PIT invariant (event/available/ingested clocks never collapsed); crypto venue ingestion lags (funding timestamps, OI snapshot times, exchange maintenance gaps) must be modeled the same way in the simulator.

strategy_name: Fear-driven asymmetric exits (cut profits short / let losses run)
mechanism: fear of losing biases attention: in winners it focuses on profit being taken away (early exit), in losers it blocks loss-confirming information (hold) — producing the classic asymmetric P&L
setup_summary: Behavioral mechanism explaining why discretionary exits degrade: the same trader holds a losing position while cutting a winning one short, purely from fear-driven attention allocation. The falsifiable claim is that discretionary exit decisions under an open position diverge from pre-committed rules in a systematic (asymmetric) direction.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: any open position where exit is left to discretion. Invalidation: system-determined exits (stop, target, still_valid) remove the discretion that fear exploits.
risk_geometry: None stated; the lesson is that exit decisions must be mechanical, not emotional.
quote: What you have just been given is an example of why the vast majority of traders cut their profits short and let their losses run. In a winning trade, the fear of losing will cause us to focus our attention on information that the market is going to take our profits away, compelling us to get out early. In a losing trade we will focus our attention on just the opposite information—anything other than that which would indicate the trade is a loser.
chapter_anchor: Ch. 10, How Memories, Associations, and Beliefs Manage Environmental Information (p. 103)
notes: Design justification for V8's deterministic stops/targets and frozen-reference still_valid checks: they exist precisely because discretionary exits under position bias are systematically wrong. Corroborates existing_family_refinement: no expert may re-evaluate its own exit emotionally; exit logic is pre-committed.

strategy_name: Revenge-trading block (last trade is irrelevant to the current opportunity)
mechanism: after losing more than intended risk, the trader seeks to 'get back', rejecting valid current profit opportunities and enlarging targets/size until the recoup target is met
setup_summary: Rule: the previous trade's P&L must never enter the current trade's decision. The book's concrete example: after a 20-tick loss with 5-tick intended risk, the trader rejects a valid 10-tick profit because 'getting back' demands 15-20 ticks — a target that no longer reflects market potential. Adversarial framing ('it's me vs the market') leads to giving money back.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: recent loss exceeding intended risk. Invalidation: any target or size adjustment keyed to recouping a prior loss is a rule violation.
risk_geometry: None stated; the rule caps discretionary adjustment of target/size by prior outcomes.
quote: For example, is a 10-tick profit enough in the trade you are currently in if you lost 20 in the last trade?... If you believe in 'getting back,' 10 won't be enough regardless of what the market is doing or telling you. You will need at least 15 and preferably 20 to make you whole.
chapter_anchor: Ch. 5, Prices Are in Perpetual Motion with No Defined Beginning or Ending (p. 47)
notes: For 24/7 perps with high leverage and instant execution, revenge size-ups/target-inflation execute within seconds. In V8 terms this is a RiskGate-adjacent admission rule: candidate generation and risk_geometry must be a pure function of point-in-time MarketState, with no path-dependence on the equity/outcome of prior episodes (consistent with rule 15: outcome data never mutates an active Expert).

strategy_name: Skill-bounded position sizing (risk comfort level; size-up after wins predicts give-back)
mechanism: position size must stay within the trader's demonstrated skill/objectivity level; sudden size-ups — especially after winning streaks, to 'prove' success — predict giving back all profits plus more
setup_summary: Rule: identify a 'risk comfort level' and expand it only as fast as the trader can maintain objective perception. Falsifiable pattern from the case study: a trader who ran a streak of 1-2 tick winners then jumped to 20 contracts lost ~$3,000 the next day — all profits plus more, in one session.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: risk/size increase beyond the level at which objectivity has been demonstrated. Invalidation: size-up driven by self-image ('prove I have arrived') is the failure signature; sizing must be a monotonic function of validated skill, not of recent wins.
risk_geometry: None stated; sizing rule only — risk per trade held at the fear-free comfort level, expanded gradually.
quote: he was reasoning that by trading a larger contract size he would make enough money to prove to himself and everyone else that he had finally arrived... The next day he lost almost $3,000.00 trading 20-contract positions. He gave back to the markets all his profits, plus more.
chapter_anchor: Ch. 8, The Three Stages to Becoming a Successful Trader (p. 69, 20-contract case study); Ch. 2, Skills to Be Acquired (p. 28, risk comfort level)
notes: V8 mapping: heat cap and per-exposure risk are frozen constants; the lesson is that a live/learning system must not let recent win streaks expand its own size. Corroborates V8 rule 15 (registry-gated learning) and the complexity budget — sizing must not be a learned, path-dependent quantity.
book: The Disciplined Trader - Developing Winning Attitudes 1990 - annotated

strategy_name: Price behavior over reasons (market is always right; post-hoc narratives are not predictive)
mechanism: price is the consensus belief of all participants acting as force; movement follows greatest force; 'reasons' given by traders after the fact are justifications/excuses with no predictive value
setup_summary: Methodology rule: build signals from observable price behavior and structure, never from post-hoc news narratives or trader-provided 'reasons'. The market is never wrong 'in what it does'; being 'right' with superior reasoning is irrelevant unless price agrees. Irrational crowd behavior is nonetheless predictable because it is driven by shared fear of scarcity and fear of missing out.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: a narrative-based or expectation-based reason to act that price does not confirm. Invalidation: if the collective force of traders moves price against the thesis, the thesis is dead regardless of its logical quality.
risk_geometry: None stated (methodology layer, not a trade geometry).
quote: If you want to learn to predict price movement, you don't need to pay attention to reasons. What you need to do is determine how the majority of traders perceive the external conditions in relationship to either their fear of scarcity, or their fear of missing out, or both. ... The market is never wrong in what it does; it just is.
chapter_anchor: Ch. 7, In the Market Environment, Reasons Are Irrelevant (p. 60); Ch. 3, The Market Is Always Right (p. 40)
notes: Foundational for V8's behavior-driven ontology: an Expert is a falsifiable hypothesis over observable MarketState behavior, and candidate episodes are validated on tape, not on narrative. In crypto perps, intraday 'reasons' (news, FUD, narratives) are abundant and cheap — this rule keeps signal construction venue-agnostic and evidence-bound.
book: The Disciplined Trader - Developing Winning Attitudes 1990 - annotated

strategy_name: Uncommitted probability assessment (evaluate market as if no position is open)
mechanism: opportunity assessment must be recomputed from current point-in-time state independent of the open position and its P&L; releasing the demand that expectations be fulfilled lets the market say when to enter and exit
setup_summary: Methodology rule: compute the opportunity as an 'uncommitted assessment of the probabilities' — the same signal logic applied whether or not a position is open. In V8 terms this is exactly the point-in-time MarketState read: candidate generation and the still_valid (dead-thesis) check are recomputed from the frozen state, never anchored to entry price or open P&L.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: any state evaluation while holding a position. Invalidation: if the assessment requires the trader's hope that price returns, the thesis is already dead; the assessment must be re-runnable as if flat.
risk_geometry: None stated (methodology layer).
quote: Releasing yourself from the demand your expectations be fulfilled exactly the way you expect them to be. Releasing yourself from the demand will allow you to shift your perspective to perceive whatever opportunities exist in the market now, as if you didn't have a trade on at all.
chapter_anchor: Ch. 8, You Create Your Experience of the Market (p. 63); Perceiving Opportunity (p. 64, 'uncommitted assessment of the probabilities')
notes: Direct architectural validation of V8: no wall-clock, frozen refs, still_valid recomputed from state, and outcome data never mutating an active expert — all implementations of 'evaluate as if you didn't have a trade on'. This is the strongest methodology anchor in Part 1 for existing design.
book: The Disciplined Trader - Developing Winning Attitudes 1990 - annotated

strategy_name: Defined conditions are the precondition for repeatable wins (random winning / random losing)
mechanism: a win produced by undefined conditions cannot be repeated or prevented; only exactly definable behavior (own and market's) enables learning to repeat wins and stop losses
setup_summary: Methodology rule: any signal or edge must be expressible as exact, observable conditions so that episodes can be reproduced and validated. The failure mode 'random winning and random losing' occurs when a trader cannot define what produced the last win, making the next trade a gamble and breeding fear/anxiety.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: a signal or outcome that cannot be restated as exact observable conditions. Invalidation: an undefined 'win' is not evidence of edge; a candidate episode must be reproducible from a point-in-time state snapshot.
risk_geometry: None stated (methodology layer).
quote: If you can't define your own behavior and that of the markets, you can't learn how to repeat your wins or prevent your losses.
chapter_anchor: Ch. 6, The Market Is an Unstructured Environment (p. 53, 'random winning and random losing')
notes: Maps to V8's evidence-bound structure: an Expert is one falsifiable hypothesis with exact trigger/invalidation/risk_geometry; without this, no registry progression (SCREENING->REPLICATION->SHADOW) is meaningful. Reinforces why the economic verdict stays NO_ECONOMIC_CLAIM until episodes are reproduced on frozen OOS.

strategy_name: Expanded timeframe for big-picture perception; objective set by market structure
mechanism: expanding the timeframe of observation increases the number of usable distinctions and the quality of opportunity assessment; profit objective should be set by what the market offers, not by personal value ('how much is enough')
setup_summary: Methodology: assess a candidate opportunity within a broader timeframe context, and let the market's structure define the profit objective ('let the market tell you how much is enough') rather than a personal target. Narrow tick-level focus serves any illusion; expanding the perspective is a component of disciplined perception.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: opportunity evaluation using only the immediate bar/context. Invalidation: a profit objective anchored to personal expectations (desired win size) rather than observable structure is a rule violation.
risk_geometry: None stated; supports setting targets from market structure instead of fixed personal goals.
quote: It will be extremely difficult to learn how to develop a perspective for the 'big picture,' by expanding your time frame perspective... You can learn how to trade where you won't be using information to justify your beliefs but rather to perceive the most likely possibilities in any given moment.
chapter_anchor: Ch. 8, You Create Your Experience of the Market (p. 63); Ch. 5 (p. 43, 'how much is enough')
notes: Supports the existing trend_pullback design (trend context on a longer frame, targets from structure not personal expectation) and the 'let the market tell you how much is enough' objective-setting principle. Relevant to perp specifics: no daily close boundary to anchor 'enough', so structure-based targets (levels, R-multiples) matter more than calendar-based targets.

strategy_name: Big-trade mentality block (honor the objective even when it is 'too small')
mechanism: rejecting a valid, structure-signaled profit objective because its size feels insulting relative to expectation; over-holding winners past the objective in the belief a bigger move is coming, then giving the profit back
setup_summary: Rule: the profit objective must be honored when taken — the book's own confession: refusing $500-$750 profits 'even when I knew that's all there was to be made' because the market felt insulting. The falsifiable claim: over-holding past a valid objective (expecting a 'big trade') systematically converts wins into give-backs.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: position at objective where remaining potential is judged by the book's observation to be exhausted. Invalidation: the decision to hold past objective must be thesis-based (structure says more), never expectation-based (the amount is 'too small').
risk_geometry: Target: set and honored per the structure; over-holding past target without a fresh thesis is the violation.
quote: my big-trade mentality was so pervasive that I would refuse to take profits of $500 or $750 in many trades even when I knew that's all there was to be made... it felt as if the market was insulting me by offering such paltry sums compared to what I needed or expected.
chapter_anchor: Ch. 1, Why I Wrote This Book (p. 19)
notes: With leverage, over-holding a winner past the objective compounds the give-back. In V8 terms this is a risk_geometry discipline rule: target_r is a frozen constant of the expert variant; letting 'expected size' mutate the target is a discretionary violation. Related to but distinct from the revenge-trading rule (that one keys targets to prior losses; this one keys holding to expected win size).

strategy_name: leverage_cap
mechanism: high leverage converts a normal adverse move into a forced liquidation; capping notional at a small multiple of equity bounds loss before the liquidation engine fires
setup_summary: Account-level risk rule: notional per position is capped at a small multiple of equity (the book's institutional benchmark is 2:1; retail was 100:1-400:1). A stop must be in place so max loss is bounded far below the point where available margin is consumed and the broker force-closes the position (the book's loss was $2,000+ on a $1,700 account because $20/pip with no stop outran the $1,200 of free margin).
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: notional-per-unit (per pip) is large relative to equity, or no stop is set. Invalidation: the exposure's worst-case loss would exhaust free margin before the stop distance; a stop distance that exceeds free-margin headroom invalidates the trade.
risk_geometry: Entry: N/A (risk gate). Stop: mandatory; must be closer than the margin-call distance. Sizing: the book states only 'we might use 2-to-1 leverage' at the institutional desk; $10/pip on $1,000 account vs. $20/pip on $1,700 account was the fatal scaling. No % rule stated.
quote: At Ernest Wellington, we might use 2-to-1 leverage. That's it. We don't mess around with crazy leverage. We'd all wash up... When your losses reached $1,200, you had used up all the available margin. So we closed your trade automatically as a service to you.
chapter_anchor: Ch. 5 'Lessons Learned' p.34 (leverage); Ch. 7 'You Never Forget Your First Margin Call' p.58-60
notes: Directly transferable to perp crypto where 100x+ leverage and a hard liquidation engine are native: the RiskGate admission rule should size notional so a 1-ATR adverse fill cannot approach the liquidation price, and every exposure must carry a stop. V8 already mandates stops in risk_geometry; this finding makes the sizing-vs-free-margin bound explicit. The counterfactual hazard — Harry held a 100+ pip adverse move with no stop and survived only via broker force-close — is the exact liquidation-cascade setup perp markets exhibit.

strategy_name: Take all system signals; think in probabilities; don't outguess the system
mechanism: Trading systems mathematically quantify past collective-behavior relationships into statistical odds; outguessing them destroys the trade sample and blocks the experience needed to believe in probable outcomes, and 2-3 consecutive losses are normal for most systems.
setup_summary: Commit to trading a well-defined-entry/exit system exactly by its rules for a set learning period, taking every signal including the losing ones; risk per trade must be an amount completely within tolerance so pain does not shut down learning; only after flawless execution becomes habit can contract size grow.
trigger_invalidation: Methodology guidance. The book's Catch-22: you won't believe in the system's odds unless you execute it long enough to internalize them, and you can't execute it long enough without the belief - the resolution is discipline, not discretion.
risk_geometry: Position sizing: risk per trade must be fully comfortable ('amount of money you risk per trade should be an amount that you are completely comfortable with'); 'keep your contract size light'.
quote: taking all the signals generated by your system is the only way you can get the firsthand experience you need to establish a belief in probable outcomes
chapter_anchor: Ch.16 'Step Four: Learning How to Execute a Trading System Flawlessly', pp.173-176
notes: Supports V8's frozen-OOS / registry discipline: the lab must consume all candidate episodes of a family, not select favorable ones, and a family's short run of consecutive losses is not itself evidence of failure. Also: 'Any identified pattern may or may not be repeating itself' - no pattern is valid until it completes.

strategy_name: Protective stops at trade initiation + expectation-based (dead-thesis) exit
mechanism: stops placed at the time of the original trade (when most objective) cap losses; a position is held only while price action confirms the entry thesis, so a contradiction or failure to confirm is an exit trigger
setup_summary: Methodology rule: place the stop when the trade is initiated (objectivity is highest then); define risk/reward parameters with the technicals before entry; stay in the position only if the market performs according to expectations - if subsequent price action contradicts or fails to confirm, exit ('Lose your opinion, not your money'). Stop placement guidance throughout the book: under the signal-candle low (hammer's low), under the supporting trendline, above the false-breakout high, or at the new high of the dark-cloud cover day. Two mottos: 'all long-term trends begin as short-term moves' and 'there is no room for hope in the market'.
trigger_invalidation: n/a - this is the risk gate itself.
risk_geometry: Stop: at trade initiation; below the signal-bar low, below the trendline, or above the false-breakout high (structure-based, not % or ATR-based in this book). No fixed target or expiry - exit on contrary price action or on a new opposing candlestick pattern (Ch.1: 'Some Japanese candlestick practitioners place a trade based on a candlestick signal and stay with that trade until another candlestick pattern tells them to offset').
quote: Stay in the position only if the market performs according to expectations. If subsequent price action either contradicts or fails to confirm these expectations, it is time to exit.
chapter_anchor: Ch. 11 sidebar 'The Importance of Protective Stops' pp.188-189; also Ch. 1 pp.7-10 and Ch. 9 p.165
notes: Directly maps to two V8 mechanisms that already exist: (1) RiskGate deterministic admission with stops in risk_geometry, and (2) the dead-thesis (still_valid) exit in lifecycle - the book's 'stay only if the market performs according to expectations' IS V8's still_valid semantic, and the 'another candlestick pattern tells them to offset' rule is a lifecycle exit trigger. 'There is no room for hope in the market' is the anti-hold-and-hope justification for deterministic stop execution. V8's STOP_FIRST simulator and frozen risk_geometry comply.
book: Japanese Candlestick Charting Techniques - A Contemporary Guide to the Ancient Investment Techniques of the Far East 1991

strategy_name: Rule of Multiple Technical Techniques (confluence at one price area)
mechanism: the more technical indicators that assemble at the same price area, the greater the chance of an accurate forecast; the coincidence is a marker of an important market juncture
setup_summary: Methodology principle (Arthur Sklarew): confluence of independent technical indicators at the same price area raises forecast accuracy. The book's canonical example: gold resistance at $425-433 derived from four independent devices (50% retracement of 1987-89 move = $430; double-bottom measured move = $425; late-1988 high = $433; Elliott 4th-wave constraint = $425) - gold peaked at $425 and the bear market resumed. Also demonstrated with candlestick clusters (Ch.10: hanging man + harami + shooting star + tweezers top within three sessions at the same highs = a short-term top). A falsifiable corollary in the book: there is always a price where the thesis is wrong (for gold, a close above $433).
trigger_invalidation: n/a - methodology. Note the book's built-in falsification rule: 'there is always a price where I will say my market view is wrong.'
risk_geometry: n/a
quote: The more technical indicators that assemble at the same price area, the greater the chance of an accurate forecast.
chapter_anchor: Part 2 intro 'The Rule of Multiple Technical Techniques' pp.172-176 and Ch. 10 'A Confluence of Candlesticks' pp.177-183
notes: For V8 this supports a registry-gated confluence/filter concept, but it must not become the absent-by-default router/shared scorer: the constitution (rule 14) keeps those out unless a registry experiment beats the single-expert baseline. The safe reading is (a) require independent confirmation before acting on a marginal candlestick signal, and (b) encode the 'price at which the thesis is wrong' as an explicit invalidation - which V8 already does via frozen refs and still_valid. The 4-indicator gold example is a strong pedagogical anchor for feature-group 'location' confluence.

strategy_name: Structural stop/target placement off swing reference points
mechanism: the stop is placed beyond the nearest defended reference so a close through it falsifies the thesis; targets are structural, not fixed-R
setup_summary: From the Ch. 20 trade journal: stops go beyond the defended reference (neckline, window, support line, hammer low) and targets go to structural levels (prior-year support, range boundary, retest of hammer lows). Position is moved to breakeven when price stalls at a nearer resistance and the short-term objective is not reached; entry direction is gated by the dominant trend (bear market => short rallies only).
trigger_invalidation: N/A - risk methodology, not a setup.
risk_geometry: Soybeans: short $6.27, stop above neckline $6.35, target $5.90 support. Corn: buy $2.68, stop under support $2.64, target $2.79 resistance. Crude: short, stop above window $17.65, target retest of hammer lows. Silver: stop moved to breakeven when $21.75 resistance stalled the move.
quote: On June 13, I recommended a short at $6.27. The stop was above the neckline at $6.35. The target was $5.90 (this was based on a support area earlier in the year).
chapter_anchor: Ch. 20 'How I Have Used Candlesticks' (pp. 281-286)
notes: Direct input to V8's risk_geometry: the book's stops are structural (beyond a defended reference) rather than fixed R-multiples - motivates a structural-stop variant of the existing stop_r parameter. Also demonstrates break-even management when a nearer objective fails and 'trend context gates direction' (refuses a bullish hammer in a downtrend).

strategy_name: Correlated simultaneous setup risk reduction
mechanism: simultaneous same-direction setups on highly correlated instruments share one underlying risk factor, so capping aggregate correlated exposure prevents a correlated drawdown that would breach the weekly cap
setup_summary: When several correlated instruments (pairwise correlation >= 0.65) print same-direction setup signals in the same bar window, halve per-trade risk (e.g., 1% -> 0.5%) so the aggregate correlated cluster stays under the weekly drawdown cap even if all signals fail together. Example given: six yen pairs all printing daily kangaroo tails -> 6 x 0.5% = 3% at risk, leaving 2% of weekly budget.
trigger_invalidation: correlation measured on a recent window; if pairwise correlation drops below the 0.65 threshold, full per-trade risk is restored
risk_geometry: per-trade risk halved to 0.5% for a correlated cluster; weekly drawdown cap 5%; aggregate cluster risk <= remaining weekly budget
quote: For simultaneous trades with a correlation of 0.65 and above, the risk is reduced to 0.5 percent per trade.
chapter_anchor: Ch 13, Risk Rules: Correlated Trades (pp. 217-218)
notes: Directly extends V8's ONE-exposure-per-(instrument,direction) rule to a correlated-cluster heat cap in RiskGate. BTC/ETH/major-alt perp returns are highly correlated and a liquidation cascade hits all BTCUSD-margined positions at once. strategy_name: Period maximum drawdown cap with first-day sizing constraint
mechanism: a hard drawdown cap on a fixed period bounds the ruin path, and per-trade sizing is derived so a single day's worst case cannot consume the whole period's budget
setup_summary: Fix a period cap (example: 5% per trading week, or per day/month depending on timeframe). Derive per-trade risk so that the worst case of all same-day signals cannot exhaust the cap on day one: with 6 signals on the first day, risk 0.65%/trade (total 3.9%), not 1%. Stop trading for the period once the cap is hit.
trigger_invalidation: cap resets at the period boundary; a cap breach halts new entries until the next period
risk_geometry: per-trade risk <= cap / max-same-day-signal-count; example cap 5% weekly; stop-trading trigger at cap breach
quote: If you have a 5 percent drawdown rule per trading week, and you have six trading signals in one day, perhaps instead of risking 1 percent per trade you risk 0.65 percent per trade for an overall risk of 3.9 percent.

strategy_name: Three-bar exit (time-stop runner exit)
mechanism: if price has not delivered in the expected direction within N bars, the edge is not materializing and time value is being lost; exit at the close
setup_summary: For runner-style trades where stop loss and profit target are one and the same, if the trade has not moved in the expected direction within three bars of entry, exit at the close of the third bar. Consistently applied (Molly's mechanical big-shadow system), accepting small winners and occasional large winners.
trigger_invalidation: trade closed at target, at stop, or at the close of the third bar whichever comes first
risk_geometry: exit at close of bar 3 on non-delivery; stop = entry risk; target = swing point/nearest zone
quote: If you are a runner, your stop loss and your profit target may be one and the same (for example, if you are using the three-bar exit).

strategy_name: Cancel pending entry if the stop level is traded before the trigger
mechanism: if price trades to the would-be stop level before the pending entry trigger fires, the setup's location premise is invalidated pre-entry
setup_summary: For a pending stop-entry (e.g., buy stop placed above a bullish kangaroo tail's high with a stop below the pattern), if the market first trades down through where the stop loss would sit, cancel the pending buy stop. The setup is dead before it triggers.
trigger_invalidation: pending order cancelled if stop level is traded before entry trigger fires; entry otherwise triggers as planned
risk_geometry: entry: buy/sell stop above/below pattern extreme; stop: beyond pattern low/high; trigger: opposite extreme
quote: If the market pushes through where the stop loss would be, it may make sense to cancel the trade. This is using market information to manage your trades, even before they occur.

strategy_name: Exit on opposite-direction signal (reversal-signal exit policy)
mechanism: an opposite-direction setup printing in the trade's location invalidates the directional thesis and should close the trade before target or stop
setup_summary: Pre-commit to an exit policy before entry: either close on any opposite-direction signal, or close only when a counter-signal prints at a zone. Example: daily NZD/USD bearish kangaroo tail short; market falls to the next zone at 0.7430 where a bullish 'almost kangaroo tail' candle prints; the naked trader closes the short there.
trigger_invalidation: exit when opposite-direction signal prints (policy-dependent: any counter-signal or counter-signal-at-zone); target/stop otherwise in force
risk_geometry: manual exit on counter-signal; stop and target still active
quote: Some naked traders will only close a trade if the market prints a reversal signal on a zone. Other naked traders will simply close a trade as soon as price action offers a counter signal, a signal in the opposite direction of the trade.

strategy_name: Rolling win-rate decay check (system potency monitoring)
mechanism: if recent-window win rate diverges from the historical win rate, the edge may be decaying; this separates a bad-luck streak from a dead system
setup_summary: Track the system's historical win rate. When a losing streak or concern arises, compute the win rate of the last 50 trades and compare it to the historical win rate; if they differ greatly, the system may be losing potency and must be re-validated on recent market data (e.g., last 3 months) before being trusted again. If the rates agree, the streak is variance.
trigger_invalidation: recent-50 win rate close to historical -> treat streak as variance, keep rules unchanged
risk_geometry: n/a (monitoring rule); re-test on a recent window before re-trusting
quote: compare your historical win rate to the win rate of the past 50 trades. If the historical win rate differs greatly from the current win rate, the trading system may be losing its potency.

strategy_name: Pre-planned drawdown retreat sequence (avoid revenge trading / cycle of doom)
mechanism: a drawdown triggers a pre-committed recovery routine instead of rule changes; mid-drawdown system redesign destroys edge and amplifies risk
setup_summary: After hitting the maximum drawdown, execute a fixed 5-step sequence: (1) step away from the trading station, (2) back-test a predetermined sample (e.g., 200 trades or a fixed date range), (3) evaluate the trading statement to separate bad luck from rule violations, (4) decide if the system still works by re-testing on recent data (e.g., last 3 months), (5) rebuild confidence slowly, demo trading if needed. Never redesign the system inside the drawdown.
trigger_invalidation: n/a
risk_geometry: n/a
quote: Without a strong structure, without rules designed to keep you from emotional revenge trading after a drawdown, you're almost certain to fall into undisciplined trading and to take on excessive risk.

strategy_name: One-edge focus: boring trading is expert trading
mechanism: concentrating on one edge reduces decision variance and system-switching waste; repeated system-switching is the primary cause of retail failure (cycle of doom)
setup_summary: Become expert at one setup and trade it repeatedly until boring; add a second system only after ~8 months of the first, and only a complementary (low-correlated) one so profits in one system tend to offset drawdowns in the other. Back-test -> forward-test demo -> small live account -> full account progression, risking 2% or less throughout.
trigger_invalidation: n/a
risk_geometry: n/a
quote: The real secret of expert traders: They focus on one market, one trading system, one edge, and they use this edge in their trading repeatedly. Profitable trading is boring.

strategy_name: Zone, split and ladder exits
mechanism: Zones act as price magnets as well as barriers, so zone levels are natural profit targets and trail anchors.
setup_summary: Zone exit: target the nearest zone, placing the take-profit a few pips short of the zone as a cushion. Split exit: half the position targets the first zone and half targets the next zone; after the first target is hit the stop moves to breakeven. Ladder exit: as each successive zone is reached, trail the stop to the previous zone, giving a one-zone cushion and letting the market breathe in trends.
trigger_invalidation: Targets and trails are mechanical; a trade ends when a zone target or the trailed stop is hit.
risk_geometry: Targets = zone levels with a few-pip cushion. Split exit moves the stop to breakeven after the first target. Ladder trail moves the stop zone-by-zone. All zone-based — requires a live, point-in-time zone map at every bar.
quote: Zones are also magnets: The market tends to be attracted to these places on the chart. In other words, zones are simultaneously price barriers and price magnets.
chapter_anchor: Ch.11 'Exiting the Trade', Zone/Split/Ladder exits pp.180-188
notes: Depends on the zone-map feature (see zone-ontology finding). In crypto, liquidation cascades can overshoot zone targets, so the cushion, the split-exit breakeven step, and the ladder give-back are the specific mechanisms to falsify.

strategy_name: Support/Resistance zone ontology and price memory
mechanism: Price reverses repeatedly at the same levels because markets have memory; a zone's importance grows with its touch count and age, and it survives across years.
setup_summary: Define a zone as the AREA where price has reversed repeatedly (not a line). Find zones on a higher-timeframe line chart — bends in the line mark zones. Zone strength scales with the number of touches; ignore minor zones (those visible one timeframe lower). Zones recycle across years. A zone is not broken until price CLOSES beyond it: intra-bar penetration ('touches deep into the beer belly') does not count as a break.
trigger_invalidation: n/a — feature-definition methodology; supplies the location feature, the close-beyond-zone break rule used by every zone-based setup, and the room-to-the-left rule for windowed extremes.
risk_geometry: n/a (location feature ontology). Zone levels drive targets, stops, and confirmation across all zone-based setups.
quote: If the market trades beyond the zone it does not mean that the market has broken the zone... most of the time if the market touches a zone, it may trade beyond the zone, but it will not close beyond the zone.
chapter_anchor: Ch.4 'Identifying Support and Resistance Zones' pp.39-70
notes: Directly informs V8's location feature group: zone-as-area, touch-count weighting, higher-timeframe zone discovery, the close-based break rule for frozen refs, and 'room to the left' for windowed extremes. The close-beyond rule is point-in-time safe.

strategy_name: Stop-gated entries filter failed set-ups
mechanism: Failed reversal set-ups retrace but almost never take out the set-up's own extreme; gating the entry on a stop beyond that extreme filters out most losers.
setup_summary: Across every naked catalyst (big shadow, kangaroo tail, big belt, last kiss, wammie/moolah), enter only with a buy/sell stop beyond the set-up candle's extreme rather than on a retracement or at market. If the market never reaches the stop level, the trade never triggers — the majority of failed-set-up losers are never entered. This is also the book's rationale for earlier entries and tighter stops than indicator-lagged signals.
trigger_invalidation: Entry is never taken on retracement into the set-up; if the entry stop is not touched, the trade is skipped (a no-trade, not a loss).
risk_geometry: Entry type = stop order beyond the set-up extreme (not market/limit). This is a risk_geometry entry-type lesson; it must be modeled against V8's STOP_FIRST and fill-at-close simulator semantics.
quote: if you decide to use buy stops and sell stops to enter your trades, you will eliminate many losing trades from your record
chapter_anchor: Ch.6 'The Big Shadow' pp.99-100; Ch.8 pp.146-148; Ch.9 p.152
notes: Transfers well to crypto, where wicks and stop-runs are frequent: a failed set-up's extreme is rarely taken out, so stop-gated entry is a cheap loss filter. The book repeats this argument in four chapters, making it a load-bearing methodology principle.

strategy_name: Back-testing integrity: no future data, few variables
mechanism: Hindsight bias, postdictive error, and parameter overfitting make backtests look profitable while the same system fails live.
setup_summary: Whether manual or automated, testing must trade only from the right-hand edge of the chart: never advance the chart and then return to take a trade; automated tests can silently leak future data (postdictive error); adding too many rules/indicators over-fits the historical data and breaks on new data. Simple systems are robust across markets and timeframes.
trigger_invalidation: n/a — methodology for the V8 lab: point-in-time MarketState, no wall clock, frozen refs, registry-gated variants.
risk_geometry: n/a (testing methodology).
quote: Seasoned traders understand how simple trading systems are robust... Using too many variables often implies that there are too many indicators in the trading system.
chapter_anchor: Ch.3 'Back-Testing Your System' pp.25-38 (hindsight bias p.32, postdictive error p.36)

strategy_name: Liquidity-thickness-conditioned order slicing (Rob Park's algo)
mechanism: Participating only when displayed depth exceeds its trailing historical average prevents the order itself from moving the market (thick books absorb flow without revealing intent).
setup_summary: Execution rule for a large order: slice it into fixed tranches on a schedule (the book's example: 100,000 shares carved into 5,000-share pieces every five minutes, never above a price cap), but only transact a child order when the displayed offer size exceeds its trailing historical average - the market is 'thick'. Refrain when the book is thin, because a smart trader will not tip intent into a thin market. Falsifiable: fills obtained on thickness-gated tranches are better than un-gated participation.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: displayed size > historical-average offered size at the child-order price. Thesis (thick books absorb flow without adverse move) invalidates if thickness-gated fills are statistically no better than thin-book fills, or if the price cap is hit repeatedly.
risk_geometry: Entry: limit child orders gated by depth-vs-historical-average; fixed tranche schedule with per-tranche price cap; no stop/target stated (it is a participation/execution rule, not a P&L setup).
quote: It only bought stock if the amount on offer was greater than the historical average of the amount offered.
chapter_anchor: Chapter 2 (Brad's Problem) - description of Rob Park's RBC algorithm
notes: Practitioner heuristic, falsifiable but not statistically validated in the book. For V8: a candidate liquidity-feature-group input (offered-size vs trailing-average depth) and a caution that thin books punish large participation - relevant to fill-quality reasoning even at 1h-bar granularity.

strategy_name: Event-granularity evidence rule (causality requires timestamped event data)
mechanism: Causal attribution of a market event is unfalsifiable unless records exist at the timescale of trading; when trading happens at microsecond scale but records are kept by the second, competing causal stories cannot be distinguished.
setup_summary: Methodological rule drawn from the 2010 flash crash: the SEC blamed a single erroneous futures sell order, but the market traded in microseconds while exchange records were second-granular (Brad's search of the SEC report: 87 hits for 'minute', 63 for 'second', 4 irrelevant hits for 'millisecond', 0 for 'microsecond'). Any causal claim built on coarser-than-event data ('someone hit a button') is unfalsifiable - 'the data didn't exist'. For V8 this is the justification for the event/available/ingested three-clock discipline and hash-bound deterministic replay.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: any causal claim about an event made from data coarser than the event timescale. Thesis (granularity determines falsifiability) invalidated only if a coarse record can be proven to uniquely determine the causal chain.
risk_geometry: Not a trading setup; a data/evidence-quality rule. V8 enforcement: append-only logs, no wall clock in replay, three never-collapsed clocks.
quote: The unit of trading was now the microsecond, but the records kept by the exchanges were by the second.
chapter_anchor: Chapter 4 (Tracking the Predator) - flash crash and Brad's word-count audit of the SEC report
notes: Directly reinforces V8's deterministic-replay and PIT rules: episode attribution is only as good as the event clock, and collapsed clocks make findings non-reproducible. Also a caution against accepting 'official' single-cause explanations for large adverse moves without microstructure-scale evidence.

strategy_name: Hidden execution-cost tax measured by controlled counterfactual experiments
mechanism: Hidden transaction costs ('the tax') are real, systematic, and invisible at the per-trade level; they are measurable only by controlled experiments that compare realized fills against a counterfactual where the mitigating mechanism is applied.
setup_summary: Measure implementation shortfall as the difference between the pre-trade quoted market and realized execution, using matched controlled trades (RBC traded 'not to make money but to test theories', with an allowed daily loss budget). Results cited: buying 10 million Citigroup shares with synchronized (front-run-proofed) arrival saved ~$29,000, under one-tenth of 1% of notional - 'the tax' - which scaled to ~$160M/day market-wide; one $9B hedge fund estimated the cost of not trading at stated prices at ~$300M/yr (~3.3%). Falsifiable: the measured saving is either above noise or it is not.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: fills on the same order with vs without the mitigating mechanism (synchronized arrival / thickness gating). Thesis (hidden costs are real and systematic) invalidates if the measured differential is within noise of zero across a large representative sample.
risk_geometry: No directional setup; a cost-model calibration lesson. Entry/target/stop not stated. For V8: the simulator's Binance cost model should include implementation shortfall / adverse selection beyond the raw fee schedule, because hidden costs materially change per-trade economics.
quote: we bought 10 million shares of Citigroup, then trading at roughly $4 per share, and saved $29,000 - or less than a tenth of 1 percent of the total price. 'That was the tax,' said Rob Park.
chapter_anchor: Chapter 2 (Brad's Problem) - Thor experiments and the presentation to T. Rowe Price; corroborated in Chapter 3/4 (the $300M hedge-fund estimate)
notes: The book's explicit evidence-methodology contribution: (a) run controlled counterfactual experiments with a bounded loss budget rather than trusting broker cost reports; (b) hidden costs are amplified by market structure (maker-taker kickbacks, routing distortions) and scale with volume; (c) extrapolating a small measured saving to market scale is a legitimate order-of-magnitude argument. Feeds V8's simulator cost model and the 'the economic verdict stays NO_ECONOMIC_CLAIM' discipline (costs must be modeled, not assumed away).

strategy_name: Methodology: prices lead fundamentals; use the tape as the discounting mechanism
mechanism: market price is a leading indicator that discounts fundamentals; lagging fundamental data should be predicted FROM price, not the reverse
setup_summary: Do not overweight lagging fundamental or media narratives against price action: 'if the technicals are bad, the fundamentals are probably just as bad'. The stock market leads the economy by 6-9 months, so a leading indicator cannot be predicted from a lagging one. For V8 this validates a behavior/tape-driven program and explains why expert inputs are price, order-flow and regime features rather than fundamentals.

strategy_name: Lifecycle rule: bearish/inverse exposure is cyclical, not a long-term holding
mechanism: bearish (inverse) positions are valid only inside the bear regime; the regime is cyclical, so short exposure must be closed when the regime flips rather than held indefinitely
setup_summary: Book states stocks spend 3 of every 4 years in uptrends, so bear funds/inverse exposure are unsuitable as long-term holdings and 'should be sold' once the bear market or correction ends - 'that's where market timing comes in'. Falsifiable lifecycle rule for V8: SHORT experts should be expiry/regime-bound; a SHORT exposure whose regime condition (e.g., price below the long-MA, downtrend intact) flips must be closed, mirroring how bear-market tools are wound down.

strategy_name: Trailing One-Bar High/Low (Tr-1BH/L) stop-entry
mechanism: Requiring the market to take out the last completed bar's extreme before entry filters out entries that would immediately reverse, and puts the initial stop close to the reversal for small known capital exposure.
setup_summary: Once the high-probability setup conditions are met (DTF momentum reversal at a price/time target zone), place a resting buy-stop one tick above the high of the last completed bar (long) or sell-stop one tick below the low (short); re-place it bar-by-bar on the new last bar until filled. Initial protective stop is one tick beyond the swing extreme made prior to entry. If the smaller time frame momentum reverses against the intended direction before fill, the order is cancelled.
trigger_invalidation: Cancel the resting order if the smaller time frame momentum makes a reversal against the trade direction, or (for shorts) reaches the oversold zone, before execution. If the swing extreme taken as the stop level is violated, the reversal thesis is voided.
risk_geometry: Entry: stop order 1 tick beyond last completed bar extreme (takeout, not bar-close). Initial stop: 1 tick beyond the prior swing high/low. Capital exposure = entry minus stop, known exactly before fill (book example: 24.75 pts on ES, judged too large, mitigated by dropping to a smaller time frame or an unleveraged ETF). No fixed expiry; entry order lives while the setup conditions hold.
quote: trail the buy-stop or sell-stop to enter the trade one tick above the high or below the low of the last completed bar. Place the initial protective stop one tick beyond the swing high or low made prior to entry.
chapter_anchor: Chapter 6, 'Entry Strategy 1: Trailing One-Bar Entry and Stop'
notes: Completely objective entry with known pre-fill exposure; 24/7 perps have no gaps, so takeout entries and one-tick-beyond stops are executable as a matter of course. In V8, this is a candidate refinement of the entry semantics of existing experts (trend_pullback currently enters NEXT_BAR_CLOSE): modeling a resting stop-order entry requires a simulator fill-model decision (canonical L1 is fill-at-close), so flag as an explicit simulator_model variant before adoption.

strategy_name: Capital exposure limits: 3% per trade, 6% aggregate, 10% monthly stop
mechanism: Capping per-trade and aggregate capital exposure keeps the account alive through losing streaks - the book states successful traders run only ~30-40% win rates, so small losses and large wins are the only path to survival; the drawdown math (20% loss needs 25% gain, 50% needs 100%) makes preservation decisive.
setup_summary: Maximum capital exposure on any single trade = 3% of available account equity; maximum exposure on all open trades = 6%; maximum acceptable monthly closed-trade loss = 10% (stop trading for the balance of the month once hit). Position size = (available capital x 3%) / (per-unit capital exposure), rounded down, where per-unit exposure = entry price - initial stop price times contract/share value. Example: $20,000 account, $325 per-contract exposure -> 2 contracts max.
trigger_invalidation: n/a - sizing rule applied to every candidate trade; if per-unit exposure is so large that even 1 unit breaches the 3% cap, pass the trade or move to a smaller timeframe (or an unleveraged instrument) to shrink exposure.
risk_geometry: The sizing formula consumes whatever risk_geometry the setup produces (entry and initial stop determine per-unit exposure); the author's framing - 'we don't determine the entry, stop, or exposure; the market does' - matches V8's design where exposure is a deterministic function of entry/stop.

mechanism: High turnover erodes net returns through transaction costs, and concentration forces deeper analysis that raises decision quality
setup_summary: Empirical claim from the book (Mauboussin 1992-2002 study): market-beating funds averaged ~30% annual turnover vs ~110% for all equity funds, held 37% of assets in top-10 names, and espoused intrinsic-value selection. strategy_name: Uncertainty-scaled margin of safety
mechanism: The required discount/edge before entering scales with the uncertainty and economic risk of the situation; higher risk demands a greater margin of safety
setup_summary: Entry-admission rule: required edge (discount, or in V8 terms required R / edge threshold) is a monotone function of uncertainty/volatility of the candidate. Falsifiable: compare per-entry outcomes across volatility buckets and require a larger edge threshold in high-uncertainty regimes.

strategy_name: Fixed-risk (percent-of-equity) sizing normalized by stop distance
mechanism: Sizing inversely proportional to per-trade stop distance equalizes dollar risk across all trades so no single trade dominates portfolio variance.
setup_summary: Risk a fixed percent of current account equity on each signal: dollar risk = pct x equity, contracts = floor(dollar_risk / stop_distance_in_dollars). On the Donchian 56-commodity system 1980-2011, raising the percent risked from 1% to 4% scaled average annual return 90.6%->503.4% with max DD 39.8%->84.5%, and gain-to-pain rose monotonically (5.17->11.21). The large-account conclusion: fixed-risk sizing delivered nearly all the risk improvement, leaving little for other money-management overlays (5.17->5.37).
trigger_invalidation: Thesis fails if gain-to-pain does not rise monotonically with risked percent, or if per-trade risk is not actually equalized (e.g., sizing floor/granularity breaks on small accounts). Once sizing normalizes risk, entry-risk caps and open-risk caps become redundant (Ch.14 finding).
risk_geometry: entry: per signal (Donchian breakout); stop: 3-standard-deviation volatility catastrophic stop (dollar risk = distance entry-to-stop x value); target: none stated here; fractions rounded down to whole contracts in the book.
quote: a fixed percentage of equity is risked on each trade. It is implemented by multiplying the fixed percentage by account equity on the day of the trade to determine the dollar amount to be risked. Then, the strategy's trade risk is used to determine the number of contracts that should be traded.
chapter_anchor: Ch.14 'Fixed-Risk Sizing', pp. 221-223, Tables 14.1, 14.10
notes: Crypto perps permit fractional sizes, removing the book's whole-contract floor problem. V8 currently sizes to a fixed stop_r (1.0R) per Expert; this supports a variant where size = (pct x equity)/stop_distance so risk is equalized across BTC, ETH, and alt perps. Funding is not priced in the book's sizing and must be added to the perp cost model.

strategy_name: Limit trade risk on entry (high entry-risk bypass)
mechanism: Bypassing entries whose initial stop distance exceeds a dollar cap keeps worst-case per-trade loss bounded and improves return-per-unit-risk in one-lot portfolios.
setup_summary: On each signal compute dollar trade risk = distance(entry, catastrophic stop) x contract value; if it exceeds a fixed cap (e.g., $2,000), bypass the trade. On the 56-commodity one-lot system, a $2,000 cap raised gain-to-pain from 7.93 to 9.11 (15% improvement) while an overly tight $1,000 cap hurt (7.02). The effect vanishes under fixed-risk sizing (Ch.14: 5.35 vs 5.36 baseline) because a 10-lot at $2,000 risk equals a 5-lot at $4,000 risk.
trigger_invalidation: The cap only helps when per-trade risk is NOT normalized by sizing. In a sized book it is redundant; in a one-lot/one-exposure book it acts as a volatility admission filter that should be re-validated per regime.
risk_geometry: entry: bar close; stop: 3-SD volatility catastrophic stop (relative to recent volatility); bypass decision made at entry only; no expiry.
quote: trades with a high trade risk are bypassed... bypassing trades with an initial stop greater than $2,000 away from the entry price increases the gain-to-pain ratio from the baseline 7.93 to 9.11, a 15 percent improvement.
chapter_anchor: Ch.12 'Limit Trade Risk on Entry', pp. 195-197; Ch.14 pp. 224-226
notes: BTCUSDT 1h ATR varies by an order of magnitude across regimes, so a per-entry risk cap in R or USD is implementable in RiskGate admission. The Ch.14 normalization caveat must be recorded: in a fixed-R, one-exposure-per-direction V8 book this caps to a volatility-regime filter rather than a sizing rule.

strategy_name: Limit open-trade risk (open-equity give-back cap, profit-taking exit)
mechanism: Exiting when distance from current price to the stop reaches a dollar/percent threshold harvests the trade's peak-to-date profit, converting open give-back into realized equity.
setup_summary: While a trade is open, monitor dollar open-trade risk = distance(current price, stop) x value; when it exceeds a threshold, exit the trade. On the 56-commodity system, exiting at >$6,000 open-trade risk beat no-exit (gain-to-pain 8.94 vs 7.93) but a tight >$4,000 cap hurt (6.66) - a U-shaped response. The percent-of-equity variant (Ch.14, capped at 8%-5% of equity) did not help the sized large-account system.
trigger_invalidation: Tight caps destroy upside (book's own >$4,000 result) and the rule is redundant where profit targets already exist (Ch.15 stock system kept a '$300 scalping profit-target' and rejected both open-risk limits).
risk_geometry: entry: as per base system; stop: catastrophic stop; exit: fixed dollar open-trade-risk threshold acting as profit-taking at peak-to-date profit; no expiry.
quote: This money management technique closes the trade when a certain dollar amount of open-trade risk is reached. Note that this can also be looked at as a form of profit-taking.
chapter_anchor: Ch.12 'Limit Open-Trade Risk', pp. 196-197, Table 12.8; Ch.14 pp. 226-227
notes: On perps there are no exchange gaps to absorb give-back and markets run 24/7, so open-equity give-back is real and measurable. In V8 taxonomy this is a THIRD exit type distinct from stops and dead-thesis (still_valid) - an episode-level give-back cap. Threshold must be frozen and is equity/leverage dependent.

strategy_name: Short correlated-surrogate hedge overlay (beta hedge)
mechanism: A short position in a highly correlated market proxy offsets the systematic beta component of a basket of longs, cutting drawdowns more than it cuts returns when the longs' edge is idiosyncratic.
setup_summary: Against N long signals in a correlated basket, hold a fixed number of short positions in a market surrogate (SPY ETF). On the Nasdaq-100 Donchian long basket, 5 longs / 2 SPY shorts raised gain-to-pain 1.78->1.90 and cut max DD $7,520->$6,589; adding 'hedge on only when >=2 active basket trades' lifted it to 2.09. The hedge only pays because the basket longs compound ~1%/2 days while the surrogate declines only marginally.
trigger_invalidation: The hedge must be gated on basket activity: when the 70-day trend filter collapses the basket to few trades the hedge bleeds (Ch.13). On perps, perpetual funding on the short leg is a recurring carry cost, and hedge beta must be re-estimated as basket composition changes.
risk_geometry: hedge legs sized like longs ($5,000 each); fixed hedge count (e.g., 2); no stated stop on hedge; hedge removed when active basket trades < threshold.
quote: let's try adding a downside hedge... sell short one or more $5,000 positions of a market surrogate like the exchange-traded fund (ETF) for S&P 500... with five longs and two shorts, profitability is reduced by about $450 per year, but average max draw-down and max draw-down are reduced even more.

notes: Natural perp analog: short BTCUSDT perp against a long basket of alt perps - directly executable with no borrow, but funding on the short leg erodes P&L and 24/7 trading means no overnight-gap protection benefit. Requires the cross_market feature group and a beta proxy series; gate hedge on active-exposure count per the book's finding.

strategy_name: Cap concurrent open-trade count
mechanism: Capping the number of concurrent positions bounds peak portfolio exposure; the benefit concentrates in drawdown control and only materializes for longer-holding systems with large open-equity give-back.
setup_summary: When open trades reach a cap, bypass new signals until one closes. Commodity one-lot book: capping at 20 trades cut max start-trade DD monotonically ($64,996->$55,932) at gain-to-pain cost (7.93->6.83); large-account sized book: cap of 30 was marginal (5.37 vs 5.36); stock book: cap 45 best (2.80). The author notes clusters of many concurrent trades carry the biggest risk/reward, so aggressive caps forfeit reward.
trigger_invalidation: Caps hurt when they bypass high-conviction cluster signals; the technique only helps strategies that hold longer with higher profit-per-trade and larger open give-back (Ch.14), and does little for fast scalpers.
risk_geometry: portfolio-level admission bypass; no per-trade change.
quote: the biggest risk/reward opportunities occur when you have a relatively large number of trades on... this money management tactic works best with longer-term trend-following strategies; those that hold trades longer and consequentially have a higher profit-per-trade as well as a larger open-equity give-back.
chapter_anchor: Ch.12 'Limit Total Number of Open Trades', p. 198, Table 12.10; Ch.14 pp. 226; Ch.15 pp. 234

strategy_name: Closed-trade-only signal attribution (no open P/L look-ahead)
mechanism: Using open-trade mark-to-market P/L in any scoring or feature feeding entries leaks information about trades already entered into future signals, inflating in-sample performance.
setup_summary: Bar-scoring using average profit over the last 10 trades dramatically raised top-score profitability; the cause was that some of the last 10 trades were still open and their running daily P/L was fed into the scoring matrix. Restricting scoring to closed trades made the profit-per-trade criterion 'only marginal'. This is the book's canonical example of subtle look-ahead bias.

strategy_name: Margin of safety asymmetry gate
mechanism: requiring a large discount between price and independently-estimated value buffers the entry against estimation error and adverse value moves
setup_summary: Before any entry, form an independent estimate of expected value and require the entry price to clear a minimum discount (roughly 25-33%) to that estimate; the setup must remain adequate even if the estimate subsequently declines by ~10%. Operates as a pre-entry admission gate overlaid on any candidate setup, not as a standalone signal.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: candidate setup where entry price is at least ~25% below (long) / above (short) the value or edge estimate. Thesis-invalidation: the discount compresses below threshold before entry, or the value estimate itself deteriorates by more than the buffer.
risk_geometry: Entry at bar close once the discount threshold is met; book gives no explicit stop/target - the margin buffer substitutes for a stop (a 25% discount survives a 10% adverse value move); holding horizon is long-term, not bar-based.
quote: There are two rules of investing, said Graham. The first rule is don't lose. The second rule is don't forget rule number one.

strategy_name: Institutional imperative / crowd-imitation avoidance
mechanism: crowd beliefs are not evidence - herding transfers the errors of the many to the follower, and contrarian conviction is only right when data and reasoning, not agreement, justify it
setup_summary: A trade thesis that depends on the continuation of a widely-shared crowd belief is suspect. Thirty-seven failed investment-banking firms were run by hard-working, high-IQ people undone by 'mindless imitation of their peers.' Before entry, verify with independent data and reasoning; 'you are right because your data and reasoning are right,' not because the crowd agrees.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: thesis relies on crowd consensus continuation (e.g., entry only justified if 'everyone keeps buying'). Invalidation: objective crowding measures show the position is not actually crowded, or independent data confirms the consensus.
risk_geometry: None - decision-process rule applied before entry; feeds thesis design, not entry/stop arithmetic.
quote: How could they get a result like that? I'll tell you how... mindless imitation of their peers.

strategy_name: Consistent operating history as regime filter
mechanism: a long steady track record of the same behavior is a relatively reliable predictor that the behavior continues, while discontinuous change destroys predictive confidence
setup_summary: Admit only instruments/regimes with a long, consistent record of the same behavior; a steady record is a relatively reliable predictor that results continue. Buffett evaluates four-to-five-year averages rather than single years, and excludes assets whose plans failed and who are fundamentally changing direction.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: candidate passes the consistency test (same behavior, comparable results, over a multi-year lookback). Invalidation: behavioral discontinuity or structural change breaks the record; single-year noise should not trigger exclusion.
risk_geometry: None - regime/selection filter applied before setup evaluation; lookback in years, not bars.

strategy_name: Leverage avoidance / heat cap
mechanism: leverage converts ordinary drawdowns into ruin - highly leveraged positions are vulnerable during economic slowdowns, so unleveraged sizing is what makes returns survivable
setup_summary: Do not use leverage to manufacture returns: 'good business or investment decisions will produce quite satisfactory economic results with no aid from leverage,' and highly leveraged entities are vulnerable during economic slowdowns. Standing rule: position size must be survivable without liquidation under adverse conditions, with a heat cap.
trigger_invalidation: Rule violation (rejection trigger): any position whose survival depends on leverage beyond what the thesis needs, or aggregate heat above the cap. Invalidation: none - standing admission rule.
risk_geometry: No entry mechanics; constrains size so stop and heat levels are reachable without forced liquidation; 'vulnerable during economic slowdowns' maps to deleveraging-cascade regimes.

strategy_name: Probability-weighted worst-case scenario analysis
mechanism: enumerating the specific scenarios that would ruin a position and requiring the worst plausible case to be survivable at the entry price is how risk gets priced into the trade
setup_summary: Before entry, enumerate the 3-5 specific scenarios that could ruin the position, assign probabilities, and verify the worst plausible case is survivable and that the entry price compensates. Wells Fargo: even if 10% of all loans (not just real estate) became problem loans at 30% loss severity, the bank still broke even - so the position was survivable.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: all enumerated catastrophic scenarios are rated low-probability AND survivable at the current price. Invalidation: any plausible scenario breaches the survivability threshold, or the probability of a ruin scenario is not negligible.
risk_geometry: No fixed stop; a survivability buffer substitutes for a stop in the worst case; entry price must compensate for weighted risk; 'A year like that - which we consider only a low-level possibility, not a likelihood - would not distress us.'

strategy_name: Circle of competence universe restriction
mechanism: investing outside the boundary of understood mechanisms makes it impossible to interpret developments and therefore impossible to decide wisely, so the defined boundary itself is the edge
setup_summary: Only trade instruments and setups whose mechanism you fully understand, and define the boundary explicitly: 'it's not how big the circle is that counts, it's how well you define the parameters.' Buffett passes on Microsoft/tech not because it is unprofitable but because he cannot project its cash flows; success is doing very few things right while avoiding big mistakes.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: the setup is inside the defined competence boundary. Invalidation: a new mechanism/industry is traded before the understanding is developed, or the boundary is left undefined.
risk_geometry: None - universe filter applied before any setup evaluation; 'An investor needs to do very few things right as long as he or she avoids big mistakes.'

mechanism: inactivity is itself a decision with a positive expected value when no candidate clears the required threshold - holding capital beats doing something stupid

Underutilized capital is 'a painful condition to be in but not as painful as doing something stupid.' The default state is no-position, and the strike lifts only on price.

mechanism: a small probability of forced distress or ruin is never acceptable regardless of expected upside; size so the worst case cannot force liquidation
setup_summary: Standing RiskGate rule: reject any exposure whose sizing implies non-trivial probability of forced liquidation or breach of the drawdown cap under historical worst-case adverse excursions. In perp terms: notional must be sized so a worst-case cascade flush (multi-ATR) does not liquidate or breach the heat cap; no expected-value maximization that risks ruin (the book explicitly rejects 99:1 leverage odds).
